questions.question: If your rear wheel locks while braking, you should:

options.text: Release the brake until the tire grips again, then brake again.
Release the brake and use only the front brake.
Keep it locked until the motorcycle stops.
Release the brake and coast to a stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep it locked until the motorcycle stops.
questions.explanation: If your rear wheel locks while braking, do not release the brake. Keep it locked until you come to a full stop.

questions.question: The effects of marijuana can last for:

options.text: No more than 15 minutes.
About an hour.
About two hours.
More than six hours.

questions.correctAnswerText: More than six hours.
questions.explanation: Smoked marijuana affects you within minutes and lasts two to four hours. Eaten marijuana takes over an hour to affect you but can last more than six hours.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect a person's blood alcohol content (BAC)?

options.text: The amount of alcohol consumed
Body weight
How quickly the alcohol was consumed
How often alcohol is consumed

questions.correctAnswerText: How often alcohol is consumed
questions.explanation: Three major factors affect BAC: the amount of alcohol consumed, how quickly you consumed it, and your body weight. Sex, physical condition, and food intake may also have some effect.

questions.question: When being passed, do not move to the far side of your lane because:

options.text: The passing vehicle may re-enter your lane too soon.
You may block another vehicle from passing you.
The side near the passing vehicle is safer.
You are more likely to feel wind from the passing vehicle on the far side.

questions.correctAnswerText: The passing vehicle may re-enter your lane too soon.
questions.explanation: When being passed, stay on the side of your lane nearest the passing vehicle. Moving to the far side may encourage the driver to re-enter your lane before it is safe to do so.

questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When traffic is light.
When traffic is heavy.
When you can see the roadway through vehicles ahead.
When weather is pleasant and clear.

questions.correctAnswerText: When traffic is heavy.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when conditions require longer stopping distances. This includes heavy traffic, bad weather, nighttime riding, when you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, and when visibility is poor.

questions.question: To reduce your reaction time, you should:

options.text: Ride slower than the speed limit.
Keep your fingers on the clutch and brake levers.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull in the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your fingers on the clutch and brake levers.
questions.explanation: To reduce your reaction time, cover the clutch and brakes by keeping your fingers ready on them. This is especially helpful in areas where hazards may appear.

questions.question: When being passed from behind, you should ride in:

options.text: The center of your lane.
The left side of your lane.
The right side of your lane.
Any part of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: The center of your lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed from behind, stay in the center of your lane. This discourages the other driver from re-entering your lane before it is safe.

questions.question: During the day, use your headlight on:

options.text: Low beam only.
High beam.
Low beam.
Alternating high and low beam.

questions.correctAnswerText: High beam.
questions.explanation: Use your high beam headlight during the day to help other drivers see you. Use high beam whenever you are not riding behind or approaching other vehicles.

questions.question: When riding a three-wheeled motorcycle through a curve, you should:

options.text: Stay in the center of the lane.
Stay on the outside of the lane.
Change your path as needed.
Use the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change your path as needed.
questions.explanation: Three-wheeled motorcycles and motorcycles with sidecars handle curves differently than two-wheeled motorcycles. The best path through a curve may not follow the curve itself. You may need to move from the outside to the inside of the curve before straightening out.

questions.question: Fatigue can be increased by:

options.text: Stopping frequently.
Riding in cool, windy weather.
Being comfortable during your ride.
Starting a ride late in the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riding in cool, windy weather.
questions.explanation: To prevent fatigue, dress to protect yourself from tiring weather like wind and rain. Limit riding to about six hours a day and take a break at least every two hours. Avoid artificial stimulants because extreme fatigue can occur when they wear off.

questions.question: When riding, you should:

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.
questions.explanation: When turning, look through the turn by turning only your head. Keep your knees against the gas tank to stay balanced while turning. Your arms should be slightly bent when holding the handgrips.

questions.question: When passing parked cars, which part of the lane should you use?

options.text: The left portion of the lane
The center portion of the lane
The right portion of the lane
Either the left or right portion of the lane

questions.correctAnswerText: The left portion of the lane
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of your lane when passing parked cars. This keeps you far from open car doors, people stepping between cars, and cars pulling out of parking spaces.

questions.question: More than half of all crashes:

options.text: Occur at speeds greater than 35 mph.
Happen at night.
Are caused by worn tires.
Involve riders with less than six months of experience on their motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Involve riders with less than six months of experience on their motorcycle.
questions.explanation: More than half of all motorcycle crashes involve riders who have had their motorcycle for less than six months.

questions.question: When traveling in a group, riders should:

options.text: Spread out to make the group easier to see.
Stay close together to make the group easier to see.
Separate occasionally.
Ride in pairs.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay close together to make the group easier to see.
questions.explanation: Riders should stay close together while keeping space to maneuver safely. Staying close makes the group easier to see and keeps riders from becoming separated. Do not ride in pairs because it does not allow enough room to maneuver.

questions.question: If you must brake in a curve, you should:

options.text: Brake more gradually than you would on a straight road.
Brake as hard as you would on a straight road.
Wait until you are out of the curve to brake.
Only use the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake more gradually than you would on a straight road.
questions.explanation: Tires have less grip when leaning than when upright. Try to straighten your motorcycle before braking. If you must brake while turning, apply the brakes smoothly and slowly.

questions.question: In traffic, motorcycles need:

options.text: Much less distance to stop than cars.
Less distance to stop than cars.
As much distance to stop as cars.
More distance to stop than cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: As much distance to stop as cars.
questions.explanation: In traffic, a motorcycle needs as much stopping distance as a car does.

questions.question: To carry a passenger, you may need to:

options.text: Adjust the shocks.
Adjust the handlebars.
Adjust the brakes.
Adjust the throttle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Adjust the shocks.
questions.explanation: The extra weight of a passenger requires adjusting the motorcycle's shocks. You should also adjust the headlight and mirrors since the motorcycle will sit at a different angle.

questions.question: To stop quickly, you should:

options.text: Use only the rear brake.
Use only the front brake.
Use both brakes.
Use the rear brake firmly while gradually increasing the front brake pressure.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes.
questions.explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, tell them to do all of the following, except:

options.text: Get on the motorcycle after the engine starts.
Sit as far forward as they can without crowding you.
Hold firmly onto your waist, hips, or belt.
Talk whenever they want.

questions.correctAnswerText: Talk whenever they want.
questions.explanation: Passengers should avoid unnecessary talking or moving so you can focus on riding. Passengers should get on only after the engine starts. They should sit forward without crowding you and hold firmly onto your waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: To discourage other vehicles from lane sharing, a motorcyclist should:

options.text: Ride in the left portion of a lane.
Ride in the center portion of a lane.
Give dirty looks if another driver moves into the lane.
Ride in a zigzag pattern to fill the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center portion of a lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center portion of the lane to discourage other drivers from trying to squeeze in next to you.

questions.question: When turning on a motorcycle, what should you do?

options.text: Press the grip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the grip opposite of the direction you want to turn.
Do not hold the grip because it is dangerous.
Do not lean the motorcycle as it is unsafe.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the grip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: When riding faster than walking speed, your motorcycle leans to turn. Press the grip in the direction you want to turn. This causes the motorcycle to lean the right way.

questions.question: Why should you not ride too far to the right when using a three-wheeled motorcycle or sidecar?

options.text: Other drivers may not see you.
You cannot pass other vehicles easily.
Other drivers may try to share your lane.
You may run off the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may run off the road.
questions.explanation: A sidecar is on the right side of the motorcycle. Riding too far right puts the sidecar at risk of leaving the road. On a three-wheeled motorcycle, the right rear wheel may also go off the road.

questions.question: When turning, what should you do?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through the turn.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look through the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look through the turn.
questions.explanation: Look through each turn to where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group ride?

options.text: In the front of the group.
Right behind the leader.
At the back of the group.
Wherever they are most comfortable.

questions.correctAnswerText: Right behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader, near the front of the group. This way, experienced riders at the back can watch them and help if needed.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid hitting an object in the road, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up before contact.
Slow down before contact.
Lean the motorcycle.
Stay seated on the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down before contact.
questions.explanation: If you cannot avoid hitting an obstacle, slow down as much as possible. Try to hit it at a 90-degree angle. Keep your motorcycle upright, rise slightly off your seat, and ease the throttle back to lighten the front wheel just before impact.
